name: Erik Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how work is changing. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I work for a company of about thirty people that makes booking software for dental clinics and physio practices. I'm on the small team that looks after the reminder texts and emails, so my day is mostly bug tickets: a clinic says patients got their reminder at 3 a.m., and I go find out why. I start at half eight, have a stand-up meeting with my team at nine, and then it's tickets until lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a bug finally makes sense. You stare at a time-zone mess for two hours and then it clicks, and that feels great. What wears me out is feeling slow. Pradeep, the senior dev I sit next to, fixes in twenty minutes what takes me a day, and I'm on the lowest pay band in the building. Our rent eats nearly half of what I take home, and my partner Lina works shifts at a care home, so we're both tired most evenings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools in your work at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. If I'm stuck on an error message I'll paste it into a chat tool and ask what it means, or get it to write a regular expression, which is a kind of search pattern I always get wrong. I don't let it write whole features. Partly I don't trust it, and partly I'm still trying to learn the job properly myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what a lot of us already say on the team chat: told you so. The demos looked amazing, and in real life it writes a test or two and gets the time zones wrong. I'd probably post something online about how the money should have gone into paying people properly instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays the same, which isn't nothing but isn't great either. I'm still the junior on low pay, still learning, still in a town with maybe three companies that hire developers. The hype dying down doesn't fix the rent or the fact that I've got less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the tickets and try to move up a pay band by next summer, which means asking Hannah, our tech lead, for a proper review. I'd use the chat tool a bit more for the boring bits, like test data. And Lina and I would keep trying to put a hundred a month aside, though we've said that before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. But it's a tired kind of relief, because the things that already stress me out are all still there. It's like a storm missing your town when the roof was already leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned saving a hundred a month. What usually stops that from happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something always comes up. Last spring it was Lina's car failing its safety test, which cost us four hundred. Before that it was my laptop charger and a dentist bill, which is funny, since I work on dental software. We have maybe three weeks of rent in the bank right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things stay as they are, what would you want from the company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper pay scale that people can see, so it's not just who asks loudest. Some of us have talked about whether a union would even be possible at a place our size. I'd join one tomorrow, but I wouldn't want to be the one who starts it, not as the newest person on the team.

say: The **AI hype** was mostly a sales pitch, and real tools still get the time zones wrong.
The money spent on hype should have gone into **paying people** properly.
think: My life stays the same: **lowest pay band**, still learning, in a town with few developer jobs.
The hype ending doesn't fix the **rent** or the **three weeks** of savings.
do: Ask Hannah for a **pay review** and aim to move up a band by next summer.
Use the chat tool more for **boring tasks** like test data.
Try again to put **a hundred a month** aside with Lina.
feel: **Tired relief**: the big threat passes, but the money stress stays.
S0.quote: The hype dying down doesn't fix the rent or the fact that I've got less than a month saved.
fieldNote: Erik's worry here is **money, not machines**; rent takes almost half his take-home pay.
He sounds pro-union but won't **go first**, because he's the newest person on the team.
His leaking-roof image shows that a plateau only removes **one extra threat**.

steps.text: Fix reminder-text bug tickets and ask Hannah for a pay review
Put a hundred a month into savings with Lina
Use the chat tool to write test data and search patterns

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to talk about this as a team, not just let management decide on its own who stays. Online I'd share stuff about tech workers organising, because I think that's where this goes. Coding is right there on the list of what AI takes over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm exactly the person this hits. Juniors fixing small bugs is the first thing the tools can do, and I'm not one of the strong juniors. If the company stops hiring and lets people leave without replacing them, the person who costs least to lose is me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get much better at the AI tools, because that's the job now, whether I like it or not. I'd ask Pradeep to show me how he uses them, maybe an hour every Friday. I'd also start looking at the bigger company two towns over, the one that does hospital rota software, and talk to the others at work about a union or at least a group that negotiates together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but not frozen. It feels like there's a door closing slowly, and I can still get through it if I move now. Some days I'd feel stupid for not learning faster before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo, who answers the support phone, for sure, because answering customers is right on that list. And the other junior, Sam, who started the same month as me. We'd basically be fighting for one seat, and I like Sam, so that would be awful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you lost the job, how long could you and Lina manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three weeks, maybe a month if we stopped everything. Lina's pay covers most of the rent but not the rest. We'd have to ask her parents for help, which I really don't want to do, or move somewhere cheaper, and there isn't really cheaper here.

say: Staff should **talk as a team** about AI instead of letting management decide who stays.
**Tech workers organising** is where this goes, and I'd share that online.
think: A junior fixing small bugs is the **first thing** the tools can replace.
If the company stops replacing leavers, I'm the **cheapest person** to lose.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly, with an hour every Friday alongside Pradeep.
Apply to the **hospital rota** software company two towns over.
Talk to colleagues about a **union** or a group that bargains together.
feel: **Scared but not frozen**, like a door closing slowly that he can still get through.
Some **regret** at not learning faster before.
S1.quote: Juniors fixing small bugs is the first thing the tools can do, and I'm not one of the strong juniors.
fieldNote: Erik names his own **weakness** plainly; he expects to be the first to go.
He reaches for **collective action** as a reflex, but his concrete moves are personal.
With **one month** of cushion, losing the job would mean asking Lina's parents for help.

steps.text: Spend an hour every Friday learning Pradeep's AI coding workflow
Apply to the hospital rota software company two towns over
Ask colleagues to form a group that bargains on pay and cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this needs government stepping in right away: a pause on mass layoffs, income support, something. I'd be in every online group calling for it. There's no way this should just be left to a few companies to decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm done as a developer within two years. My whole job is thinking work at a screen; there's nothing hands-on in it at all, so the robots arriving later in 2031 doesn't buy me anything. The only three years of shelter is if I get out of the screen work and into something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd stop pretending I can out-learn it and start a trade, probably an electrician's course at the college in the evenings, because that work stays with people until about 2031. I'd cut our streaming and the gym and move every spare bit into savings. And I'd join whatever union or campaign is pushing for income support, because three years of shelter isn't a plan, it's a delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I'd lie awake doing sums. I'm twenty-seven and I'd be starting over with no money, and the new thing only lasts three years before the robots arrive too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lina that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her that her job is probably safer than mine for once, because looking after old people is hands-on. That would be a strange conversation, since I've always been the one who was meant to earn more one day. Then we'd make a list of what to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a trade only buys three years. Why take it at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because three years of wages is three years of rent, and maybe by then the government has worked something out. I'm not doing it because I think wiring houses is safe forever. I'm doing it because sitting at my desk waiting is worse.

say: Government must step in **right away** with a pause on mass layoffs and **income support**.
A few companies shouldn't get to decide this **alone**.
think: My job is **all screen work**, so I expect to be finished within two years.
Robots arriving in **2031** only shelters people who move into **hands-on work**.
do: Start an **evening electrician's course** at the local college.
Cut **streaming and the gym** and move every spare bit into savings.
Join a union or **campaign** pushing for income support.
feel: **Sick and sleepless**, doing sums at night about starting over at twenty-seven with no money.
S2.quote: Three years of wages is three years of rent, and maybe by then the government has worked something out.
fieldNote: Erik sees the **3-year gap** before robots as the only shelter outside screen work.
He flips the household roles: Lina's **care work** is now the safer income.
He calls the trade **a delay**, not a plan, and still takes it.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening electrician's course at the town college
Cancel streaming and the gym and save the difference
Join a union campaign for income support during layoffs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much what I said for the fast one, but I'd be calmer saying it. Five years is enough time to get laws in place if people push. I'd post about that and go to whatever meetings the union holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still means my coding job ends, just in 2031 instead of 2028. The difference is I'd have time to finish something properly. With five years I could do a full apprenticeship and get qualified before the robots even arrive in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the developer job for now, because I need the money, and use AI tools much more so I last as long as possible. In the evenings I'd start an electrician's apprenticeship course, two nights a week, so I'm qualified by about 2029. I'd also try to save a real cushion, three months, by selling my old gaming PC and the second bike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. Being given five years feels like being given a deadline instead of being pushed off a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your boss you were training for something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not at first. Hannah's fair, but if the company has to cut people, I don't want to hand them a reason. Maybe once I'm close to qualified I'd be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI more to last longer. Doesn't that speed up your own replacement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I've thought about that. But if I don't, someone else does, and they keep the job while I don't. It feels a bit like helping build the thing that pushes me out, and I hate that, but rent is rent.

say: Five years is **enough time** to get laws in place if people push.
I'd go to **union meetings** and post about protections for workers.
think: My **coding job** still ends, just in **2031** instead of 2028.
Five years lets me get **fully qualified** in a trade before robots arrive in 2034.
do: Keep the developer job and use **AI tools** heavily to last longer.
Study for an **electrician's apprenticeship** two nights a week, qualified by about 2029.
Build a **three-month cushion** by selling the gaming PC and second bike.
feel: **Anxious but breathing**, like being given a deadline rather than pushed off a cliff.
S3.quote: Being given five years feels like being given a deadline instead of being pushed off a cliff.
fieldNote: The extra years turn Erik's trade plan from a **stopgap** into a real qualification.
He admits using AI **speeds his own replacement**, and does it anyway for the rent.
He would **hide his training** from his tech lead to avoid being first cut.

steps.text: Use AI coding tools daily to stay useful on the reminders team
Study for an electrician's apprenticeship two evenings a week
Sell the old gaming PC and second bike to build savings
Attend union meetings on protections for tech workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for us to do this right, as a society. Shorter working weeks, retraining paid for by the companies making the money, that kind of thing. I'd be one of the people pushing for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years gives me a real career, just maybe not this one forever. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands. That's young enough to have switched once already and still have something to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in software and get properly good at working with AI over the next three or four years, because there'd still be years of that work. I'd save, slowly, maybe build to two months in the first year. Around 2030 I'd decide whether to go into a trade or into something like teaching people to use these systems, depending on what's growing then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than in the others. There's time to make mistakes and fix them, which I don't usually have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you and Lina's plans with ten years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about kids around thirty. With two years I'd say no way. With ten, I think we'd still do it, but we'd want a bigger cushion first and maybe live nearer her parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this version that still keeps you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just that ten years can feel like plenty and then suddenly it's year eight and you haven't done anything. I know myself, I wait. So I'd want something that forces me, like signing up for a course with a start date.

say: Ten years is enough time to do this **fairly**, with **shorter weeks** and company-paid retraining.
I'd be one of the people **pushing** for those changes.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd still be young enough to switch careers once.
Ten years gives me **a real career**, just maybe not this one forever.
do: Get properly good at **working with AI** in software over three or four years.
Build savings slowly to **two months** in the first year.
Decide around **2030** between a trade and teaching people to use AI.
feel: **Uneasy but hopeful**, because there's time to make mistakes and fix them.
S4.quote: Ten years can feel like plenty and then suddenly it's year eight and you haven't done anything.
fieldNote: Erik still marks himself **anxious**: thin savings and a weak position don't vanish with time.
He knows he **procrastinates** and wants a course with a start date to force him.
Plans for **children** survive in this version but not the two-year one.

steps.text: Practise AI-assisted coding on real tickets for the next three years
Save until there are two months of rent in the bank
Book a careers course with a fixed start date for 2030
Wait until about 2030 before choosing a trade or teaching

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. I'd have two years, no savings, and a job that's all screen work. What would help is income support that kicks in fast, and paid places on trade courses, so people like me aren't choosing between rent and retraining.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how lonely it would be. Everyone talks about jobs, but if Pradeep and Sam and Jo all go, that's my whole day gone. Work is where most of my friends are. Nobody pays you to keep your friends.

headlineQuote: Nobody pays you to keep your friends.
portrait: Erik, 27, fixes **reminder-text bugs** for a small company making booking software for dental and physio clinics.
He's on the **lowest pay band**, rents with his partner Lina, a care-home worker, and has about three weeks saved.
He's **pro-union** and wants government action, but as the newest hire he won't be first to organise.
In the AGI pictures he plans an **electrician's course**, seeing the 3-year robot gap as shelter for hands-on work.
More time makes him calmer but not calm; he knows he **waits too long** and wants deadlines that force him.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: two years, no savings and a job that is entirely screen work.
whatWouldHelp: Fast **income support** and paid trade courses, so retraining doesn't compete with rent.
